claim: Auditory-induced defensive flight behavior can be facilitated by somatosensory input in mice.
source: In this study, we report that auditory-induced defensive flight behavior can be facilitated by somatosensory input in mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The cross-modality modulation of defensive behavior is mediated by the projection from the primary somatosensory cortex (SSp) to the ventral sector of zona incerta (ZIv).
source: This cross-modality modulation of defensive behavior is mediated by the projection from the primary somatosensory cortex (SSp) to the ventral sector of zona incerta (ZIv).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that silencing SSp or ZIv abolishes the enhancement effect (Figure 1D-F, Figure 2F-H), and optogenetic activation of SSp-ZIv projection enhances flight (Figure 2C-E).

claim: Parvalbumin (PV)-positive neurons in ZIv receive direct input from SSp.
source: Parvalbumin (PV)-positive neurons in ZIv, receiving direct input from SSp, mediate the enhancement of the flight behavior via their projections to the medial posterior complex of thalamus (POm).
evidence: This is supported by slice recording data showing monosynaptic EPSCs in ZIv PV+ neurons upon optogenetic stimulation of SSp axons (Figure 2I-K).

claim: ZIv PV+ neurons mediate the enhancement of flight behavior via their projections to the medial posterior complex of thalamus (POm).
source: Parvalbumin (PV)-positive neurons in ZIv, receiving direct input from SSp, mediate the enhancement of the flight behavior via their projections to the medial posterior complex of thalamus (POm).
evidence: This is supported by data showing that activation of ZIv-POm projection enhances flight (Figure 4F-H) and silencing this projection blocks tactile enhancement (Figure 4I-K).

claim: Defensive behaviors are critical for animal survival.
source: Defensive behaviors are critical for animal survival.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific knowledge in the field of behavioral neuroscience.

claim: Environmental contexts, properties and intensity of threats, as well as expectations from past experiences can all modulate the form as well as the magnitude of defensive behaviors.
source: They are dynamic and adaptive, as environmental contexts, properties and intensity of threats, as well as expectations from past experiences can all modulate the form as well as the magnitude of defensive behaviors (Fanselow, 1994; Gross and Canteras, 2012; Tovote et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Threat signals in the external environment are sensed by different sensory modalities through distinct sensory pathways to initiate appropriate defensive behaviors.
source: Threat signals in the external environment are sensed by different sensory modalities through distinct sensory pathways to initiate appropriate defensive behaviors.
evidence: This is a general statement based on established knowledge in sensory neuroscience.

claim: Previous studies have mostly been focused on defensive behaviors initiated under stimulation of one individual sensory modality.
source: Previous studies have mostly been focused on defensive behaviors initiated under stimulation of one individual sensory modality (Fanselow and LeDoux, 1999; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neural circuit bases for the potential cross-modality interactions in defensive behaviors are largely unknown.
source: However, neural circuit bases for the potential cross-modality interactions in defensive behaviors are largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, based on the authors' assessment of existing literature.

claim: The vibrissal system is crucial to behaviors such as navigation and exploration.
source: The vibrissal system is crucial to behaviors such as navigation and exploration (Carvell and Simons, 1990; Diamond et al., 2008), and rodents frequently collect information from surroundings using their whiskers (Prigg et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Rodents frequently collect information from surroundings using their whiskers.
source: The vibrissal system is crucial to behaviors such as navigation and exploration (Carvell and Simons, 1990; Diamond et al., 2008), and rodents frequently collect information from surroundings using their whiskers (Prigg et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Zona incerta (ZI) is a major GABAergic subthalamic nucleus consisting of heterogeneous groups of cells.
source: Zona incerta (ZI) is a major GABAergic subthalamic nucleus consisting of heterogeneous groups of cells.
evidence: This is a statement based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: In rodents, four (rostral, ventral, dorsal, caudal) sectors of ZI can be loosely defined based on neurochemical expression patterns.
source: In rodents, four (rostral, ventral, dorsal, caudal) sectors of ZI can be loosely defined based on neurochemical expression patterns (Ma et al., 1997; Mitrofanis et al., 2004), and it has been suggested that different sectors might be involved in different circuits and functions (Liu et al., 2017; Plaha et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Different sectors of ZI might be involved in different circuits and functions.
source: In rodents, four (rostral, ventral, dorsal, caudal) sectors of ZI can be loosely defined based on neurochemical expression patterns (Ma et al., 1997; Mitrofanis et al., 2004), and it has been suggested that different sectors might be involved in different circuits and functions (Liu et al., 2017; Plaha et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: GABAergic neurons in the rostral sector of ZI (ZIr) play a role in reducing defensive behavior in an experience-dependent manner.
source: Our recent study has shown that GABAergic neurons in the rostral sector of ZI (ZIr) play a role in reducing defensive behavior in an experience-dependent manner (Chou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: ZI receives inputs from various cortical areas including the primary somatosensory cortex (SSp).
source: ZI receives inputs from various cortical areas including the primary somatosensory cortex (SSp) (Kolmac et al., 1998; Shammah-Lagnado et al., 1985) as well as from the brainstem trigeminal nucleus that relays vibrissal information (Roger and Cadusseau, 1985; Smith, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ZI receives inputs from the brainstem trigeminal nucleus that relays vibrissal information.
source: ZI receives inputs from various cortical areas including the primary somatosensory cortex (SSp) (Kolmac et al., 1998; Shammah-Lagnado et al., 1985) as well as from the brainstem trigeminal nucleus that relays vibrissal information (Roger and Cadusseau, 1985; Smith, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Deflecting whiskers directly induces neuronal activity in the ventral sector of ZI (ZIv).
source: A recent study has demonstrated that deflecting whiskers directly induces neuronal activity in the ventral sector of ZI (ZIv) (Urbain and Deschênes, 2007), where parvalbumin (PV) positive neurons are enriched (Kolmac and Mitrofanis, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Parvalbumin (PV) positive neurons are enriched in ZIv.
source: A recent study has demonstrated that deflecting whiskers directly induces neuronal activity in the ventral sector of ZI (ZIv) (Urbain and Deschênes, 2007), where parvalbumin (PV) positive neurons are enriched (Kolmac and Mitrofanis, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Tactile stimulation enhanced the running induced by noise sound in head-fixed mice.
source: We found that tactile stimulation enhanced the running induced by noise sound (Figure 1A, right), as demonstrated by the increased peak speed (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and total travel distance (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-C and supplementary figures.

claim: Tactile stimulation increased peak speed of noise-induced running.
source: We found that tactile stimulation enhanced the running induced by noise sound (Figure 1A, right), as demonstrated by the increased peak speed (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and total travel distance (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tactile stimulation increased total travel distance of noise-induced running.
source: We found that tactile stimulation enhanced the running induced by noise sound (Figure 1A, right), as demonstrated by the increased peak speed (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and total travel distance (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The temporal profile of the behavioral response was not significantly affected by tactile stimulation.
source: The temporal profile of the behavioral response was not significantly affected, as shown by the quantifications of onset latency and time to peak (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data referenced in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Silencing the SSp contralateral to the whiskers being deflected by infusing muscimol removed the difference in speed between conditions without and with whisker stimulation.
source: Silencing the SSp contralateral to the whiskers being deflected by infusing a GABA receptor agonist, muscimol (Figure 1D, left), removed the difference in speed between conditions without and with whisker stimulation (Figure 1D–F), without altering the response temporal profile (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The tactile enhancement of running is mediated mainly through SSp.
source: This suggests that the tactile enhancement of running is mediated mainly through SSp.
evidence: This is an inference based on the muscimol silencing experiment showing that SSp inactivation abolishes the tactile enhancement effect.

claim: Trimming of all whiskers of the animal significantly decreased the average speed of the flight through the channel in a two-chamber test.
source: Trimming of all whiskers of the animal significantly decreased the average speed of the flight through the channel (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that tactile information through whiskers can indeed enhance flight behavior in a more natural condition.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Tactile information through whiskers can enhance flight behavior in a more natural condition.
source: Trimming of all whiskers of the animal significantly decreased the average speed of the flight through the channel (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that tactile information through whiskers can indeed enhance flight behavior in a more natural condition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the whisker trimming experiment in freely moving animals.

claim: SSp projects to ZIv.
source: Previous studies have suggested that SSp projects to ZIv (Kolmac et al., 1998; Shammah-Lagnado et al., 1985), and that ZIv neurons respond to whisker deflections (Urbain and Deschênes, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and confirmed by the authors' tracing experiments shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: ZIv neurons respond to whisker deflections.
source: Previous studies have suggested that SSp projects to ZIv (Kolmac et al., 1998; Shammah-Lagnado et al., 1985), and that ZIv neurons respond to whisker deflections (Urbain and Deschênes, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Profuse fluorescence-labeled axons from SSp were found in ZIv, but few in other ZI sectors.
source: We found profuse fluorescence-labeled axons in ZIv, but few in other ZI sectors (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the SSp axons in ZIv enhanced noise-induced running.
source: The optogenetic activation of the SSp axons in ZIv enhanced noise-induced running (Figure 2C–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B) without affecting the response temporal profile (Supplementary file 1), but by itself had no effect on the baseline locomotion speed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SSp axons in ZIv by itself had no effect on the baseline locomotion speed.
source: The optogenetic activation of the SSp axons in ZIv enhanced noise-induced running (Figure 2C–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B) without affecting the response temporal profile (Supplementary file 1), but by itself had no effect on the baseline locomotion speed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Infusing muscimol into ZIv bilaterally abolished the enhancement of flight response by whisker stimulation.
source: Infusing muscimol into ZIv bilaterally abolished the enhancement of flight response by whisker stimulation (Figure 2F–H) without affecting the response temporal profile (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: Activation of the SSp-ZIv projection is sufficient and necessary for the tactile enhancement of auditory-induced flight response.
source: Together, these results suggest that activation of the SSp-ZIv projection is sufficient and necessary for the tactile enhancement of auditory-induced flight response.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined results of optogenetic activation and muscimol silencing experiments.

claim: Blue light pulses evoked monosynaptic excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in most ZIv PV+ neurons recorded with tetrodotoxin (TTX) and 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) present in the bath solution.
source: We observed that blue light pulses evoked monosynaptic excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in most ZIv PV+ neurons recorded with tetrodotoxin (TTX) and 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) present in the bath solution.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by slice recording data shown in Figure 2J-K.

claim: The EPSC evoked by blue light in ZIv PV+ neurons could be blocked by an AMPA receptor blocker, CNQX.
source: The EPSC could be blocked by an AMPA receptor blocker, 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (CNQX) (Figure 2J–K).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by slice recording data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: ZIv PV+ neurons receive direct excitatory input from SSp.
source: These results indicate that ZIv PV+ neurons receive direct excitatory input from SSp.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the monosynaptic EPSC recordings shown in Figure 2J-K.

claim: Activation of ZI PV+ neurons enhanced flight response induced by noise stimulation.
source: We found that activation of ZI PV+ neurons enhanced flight response induced by noise stimulation (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E), whereas suppression of these neurons reduced the flight response (Figure 3D–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Suppression of ZI PV+ neurons reduced the flight response.
source: We found that activation of ZI PV+ neurons enhanced flight response induced by noise stimulation (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E), whereas suppression of these neurons reduced the flight response (Figure 3D–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by optogenetic suppression data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Neither activation nor suppression of ZIv PV+ neurons alone significantly affected the baseline locomotion.
source: As a control, neither activation nor suppression of ZIv PV+ neurons alone significantly affected the baseline locomotion (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by control data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of ZIv PV+ neurons prevented the enhancement of noise-induced flight response by whisker stimulation.
source: The chemogenetic silencing of ZIv PV+ neurons prevented the enhancement of noise-induced flight response by whisker stimulation (Figure 3G–I) without affecting the response temporal profile (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by DREADDi silencing data shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: ZIv PV+ neurons respond to both noise sound and whisker deflections.
source: We found that these neurons responded to both noise sound and whisker deflections and that concurrent whisker deflections increased the response level to noise (Figure 3K–L).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by optrode recording data shown in Figure 3K-L.

claim: Concurrent whisker deflections increased the response level of ZIv PV+ neurons to noise.
source: We found that these neurons responded to both noise sound and whisker deflections and that concurrent whisker deflections increased the response level to noise (Figure 3K–L).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by optrode recording data shown in Figure 3K-L.

claim: ZIv PV+ neurons can integrate tactile and auditory inputs.
source: This result indicates that ZIv PV+ neurons can integrate tactile and auditory inputs and that tactile input plays a faciliatory role, consistent with the behavioral results.
evidence: This is an inference based on the optrode recording data showing responses to both modalities and their interaction.

claim: Tactile input plays a faciliatory role in ZIv PV+ neuron responses.
source: This result indicates that ZIv PV+ neurons can integrate tactile and auditory inputs and that tactile input plays a faciliatory role, consistent with the behavioral results.
evidence: This is an inference based on the optrode recording data showing enhanced responses with concurrent whisker stimulation.

claim: The tactile enhancement of flight behavior is mediated primarily by ZIv PV+ neurons.
source: Altogether, our results strongly suggest that the tactile enhancement of flight behavior is mediated primarily by ZIv PV+ neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined results of optogenetic, chemogenetic, and recording experiments.

claim: Two targets, the medial posterior complex of thalamus (POm) and superior colliculus (SC), received the strongest projections from ZIv PV+ neurons.
source: Consistent with previous results (Barthó et al., 2002; Trageser and Keller, 2004), we found that two targets, the medial posterior complex of thalamus (POm) and superior colliculus (SC), received the strongest projections from ZIv PV+ neurons (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, as well as citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation of the ZIv-SC projection did not significantly change the flight speed.
source: While activation of the ZIv-SC projection did not significantly change the flight speed (Figure 4C–E), that of the ZIv-POm projection significantly increased the flight speed (Figure 4F–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B), similar to the activation of ZIv PV+ neuron cell bodies.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by optogenetic data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Activation of the ZIv-POm projection significantly increased the flight speed.
source: While activation of the ZIv-SC projection did not significantly change the flight speed (Figure 4C–E), that of the ZIv-POm projection significantly increased the flight speed (Figure 4F–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B), similar to the activation of ZIv PV+ neuron cell bodies.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by optogenetic data shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: Activation of the ZIv-POm projection alone did not change the baseline locomotion speed.
source: As a control, activation of the ZIv-POm projection alone did not change the baseline locomotion speed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by control data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Chemogenetic silencing of the ZIv-POm projection prevented the enhancement of flight speed by whisker stimulation.
source: The chemogenetic silencing of the ZIv-POm projection prevented the enhancement of flight speed by whisker stimulation (Figure 4I–K).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by DREADDi silencing data shown in Figure 4I-K.

claim: The projection of ZIv PV+ neurons to POm primarily mediates the enhancement of sound-induced flight behavior by tactile stimulation.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that the projection of ZIv PV+ neurons to POm primarily mediates the enhancement of sound-induced flight behavior by tactile stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined results of optogenetic activation and chemogenetic silencing of the ZIv-POm projection.

claim: Tactile input through whisker deflections can modulate defensive flight via the SSp-ZIv-POm pathway.
source: Together, our data suggest that tactile input through whisker deflections can modulate defensive flight via the SSp-ZIv-POm pathway.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Rodents frequently use their whiskers to locate and identify objects.
source: Rodents frequently use their whiskers to locate and identify objects (O'Connor et al., 2013; Pammer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In complex sensory environments, whiskers are essential for rodents to gather information from surroundings as to guide their behaviors during exploration and navigation.
source: In complex sensory environments, whiskers are essential for them to gather information from surroundings as to guide their behaviors during exploration and navigation (Ahl, 1986; Diamond et al., 2008; Sofroniew et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Specific somatosensory input plus loud sound may indicate the immediate proximity of a predator.
source: When escape behavior is concerned, specific somatosensory input plus loud sound may indicate the immediate proximity of a predator, and enhancement of flight at such moments will greatly increase survival chances of prey animals.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the ecological significance of the observed phenomenon.

claim: Enhancement of flight at moments when somatosensory input plus loud sound occur will greatly increase survival chances of prey animals.
source: When escape behavior is concerned, specific somatosensory input plus loud sound may indicate the immediate proximity of a predator, and enhancement of flight at such moments will greatly increase survival chances of prey animals.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the adaptive value of the observed behavior.

claim: Information conveyed by the somatosensory system about the environment could be extremely useful for the prey animal to quickly choose an effective escape route.
source: In addition, information conveyed by the somatosensory system about the environment could be extremely useful for the prey animal to quickly choose an effective escape route (Diamond et al., 2008; Douglass et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and represents a speculative interpretation of the functional significance.

claim: The ability to integrate somatosensory input and modulate defensive flight behavior accordingly is beneficial for animals to avoid dangers.
source: Therefore, the ability to integrate somatosensory input and modulate defensive flight behavior accordingly is beneficial for animals to avoid dangers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and their ecological context.

claim: Somatosensory input from whiskers can enhance auditory-induced flight response.
source: Here, we show that somatosensory input from whiskers can enhance auditory-induced flight response.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: In freely moving mice, trimming of whiskers reduces the efficiency of their escape from a source of loud noise by crossing through a channel.
source: Indeed, in freely moving mice, trimming of whiskers reduces the efficiency of their escape from a source of loud noise by crossing through a channel, indicating a faciliatory role of the tactile input.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The tactile-auditory cross-modality modulation relies on conveying somatosensory information primarily from SSp to ZI.
source: The tactile-auditory cross-modality modulation relies on conveying somatosensory information primarily from SSp to ZI.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing the necessity of SSp and ZI for the cross-modality effect.

claim: ZI has been implicated in maintaining normal posture and locomotor functions.
source: ZI has been implicated in maintaining normal posture and locomotor functions (Edwards and Isaacs, 1991), as it sends dense projections to motor-related thalamic and brainstem nuclei (Kolmac et al., 1998; Shaw and Mitrofanis, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ZI sends dense projections to motor-related thalamic and brainstem nuclei.
source: ZI has been implicated in maintaining normal posture and locomotor functions (Edwards and Isaacs, 1991), as it sends dense projections to motor-related thalamic and brainstem nuclei (Kolmac et al., 1998; Shaw and Mitrofanis, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The somatosensory input to ZI has a potential to influence motor functions.
source: The somatosensory input to ZI thus has a potential to influence motor functions (Périer et al., 2002; Supko et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SSp projections to ZI are mainly concentrated in ZIv.
source: In this study, we show that SSp projections to ZI are mainly concentrated in ZIv, where PV+ neurons are a major cell type (Mitrofanis, 2005; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 2B and citations to previous literature.

claim: PV+ neurons are a major cell type in ZIv.
source: In this study, we show that SSp projections to ZI are mainly concentrated in ZIv, where PV+ neurons are a major cell type (Mitrofanis, 2005; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PV+ neurons in ZIv receive direct excitatory input from SSp and respond to whisker deflections.
source: Consistent with this projection, PV+ neurons in ZIv receive direct excitatory input from SSp and respond to whisker deflections.
evidence: This claim is supported by slice recording data (Figure 2I-K) and optrode recording data (Figure 3K-L).

claim: Tactile-auditory integration takes place in ZIv PV+ neurons.
source: Concurrent whisker deflections also increase their responses to sound, indicating that tactile-auditory integration takes place in ZIv PV+ neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the optrode recording data showing enhanced responses to combined stimuli.

claim: Activating SSp-ZIv axon terminals or ZIv PV+ neurons directly enhances auditory-induced flight.
source: Activating SSp-ZIv axon terminals or ZIv PV+ neurons directly enhances auditory-induced flight, while silencing the PV+ neurons abolishes the enhancement of flight by tactile stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic activation data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Silencing ZIv PV+ neurons abolishes the enhancement of flight by tactile stimulation.
source: Activating SSp-ZIv axon terminals or ZIv PV+ neurons directly enhances auditory-induced flight, while silencing the PV+ neurons abolishes the enhancement of flight by tactile stimulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by chemogenetic silencing data shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: Via the SSp-ZIv pathway mediated mainly by ZIv PV+ neurons, somatosensory input can modulate motor functions in defensive behavior.
source: Therefore, our data demonstrate that via the SSp-ZIv pathway mediated mainly by ZIv PV+ neurons, somatosensory input can modulate motor functions in defensive behavior.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data.

claim: Different ZI sectors are dominated by distinct cell types.
source: Different ZI sectors are dominated by distinct cell types (Mitrofanis, 2005; Ricardo, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Different ZI cell types or sectors may exhibit different connectivity patterns.
source: It has been suggested that different ZI cell types or sectors may exhibit different connectivity patterns (Mitrofanis, 2005), contributing to ZI's multiplex roles in various physiological functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Activation of GABAergic neurons in the rostral sector of ZI (ZIr) can induce binge-like eating via its projections to the periventricular nucleus of thalamus.
source: For example, it has been shown that activation of GABAergic neurons in the rostral sector of ZI (ZIr), which are likely PV-negative, can induce binge-like eating via its projections to the periventricular nucleus of thalamus (Zhang and van den Pol, 2017), while Lhx6-expressing neurons in ZIv, which are also PV-negative, can regulate sleep through their projections to hypothalamic areas (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Lhx6-expressing neurons in ZIv can regulate sleep through their projections to hypothalamic areas.
source: For example, it has been shown that activation of GABAergic neurons in the rostral sector of ZI (ZIr), which are likely PV-negative, can induce binge-like eating via its projections to the periventricular nucleus of thalamus (Zhang and van den Pol, 2017), while Lhx6-expressing neurons in ZIv, which are also PV-negative, can regulate sleep through their projections to hypothalamic areas (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Activation of ZIr GABAergic neurons reduces noise-induced flight via their projections to the periaqueductal gray (PAG).
source: Indeed, we have previously shown that activation of ZIr GABAergic neurons reduces noise-induced flight via their projections to the periaqueductal gray (PAG) (Chou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The effect of activating ZIr GABAergic neurons is opposite to that of activating ZIv PV+ neurons.
source: This effect is opposite to that of activating ZIv PV+ neurons, which have few projections to PAG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparison based on the current study's findings and previous work, supported by anatomical data.

claim: ZIv PV+ neurons have few projections to PAG.
source: This effect is opposite to that of activating ZIv PV+ neurons, which have few projections to PAG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both silencing the PV+ neuron output and silencing the amygdala inhibitory input to the PV+ neurons disrupt fear memory acquisition as well as recall of remote fear memory.
source: More recently, using conditioned freezing response as a model, a study of ZIv PV+ neurons has shown that both silencing the PV+ neuron output and silencing the amygdala inhibitory input to the PV+ neurons disrupt fear memory acquisition as well as recall of remote fear memory (Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: ZIv PV+ neurons can play a role in regulating both innate and learned defensive behaviors.
source: Therefore, ZIv PV+ neurons can play a role in regulating both innate and learned defensive behaviors, which are generated under different contexts and likely engage different upstream pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current study's findings on innate behavior and previous work on learned behavior.

claim: POm is known to project to the striatum to modulate locomotion.
source: POm is known to project to the striatum to modulate locomotion (Ohno et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The inhibitory nature of striatal neurons makes them a good candidate for engaging disinhibition of distant output responses.
source: The inhibitory nature of striatal neurons makes them a good candidate for engaging disinhibition of distant output responses (Grillner et al., 2005; Kreitzer and Malenka, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and represents a speculative interpretation.

claim: The noise-induced flight behavior depends on a pathway from the auditory cortex (AC) to the cortex of inferior colliculus (ICx) and then to PAG.
source: Furthermore, we have shown previously that the noise-induced flight behavior depends on a pathway from the auditory cortex (AC) to the cortex of inferior colliculus (ICx) and then to PAG (Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: It is possible that the ZIv-POm pathway directly or indirectly connect to midbrain areas downstream of the AC-ICx-PAG pathway.
source: It is possible that the ZIv-POm pathway directly or indirectly connect to midbrain areas downstream of the AC-ICx-PAG pathway (Marchand and Hagino, 1983; Roseberry et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Somatosensory information carried by the ZIv-POm pathway can modulate the auditory-induced behavior mediated by the AC-ICx-PAG pathway.
source: As such, somatosensory information carried by the ZIv-POm pathway can modulate the auditory-induced behavior mediated by the AC-ICx-PAG pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how the observed circuit might function in the broader context.

claim: ZI has complex input and output connectivity patterns.
source: Overall, ZI has complex input and output connectivity patterns (Chou et al., 2018; Nicolelis et al., 1992; Roger and Cadusseau, 1985; Shammah-Lagnado et al., 1985; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature including the authors' own work.

claim: Through convergent and divergent connectivity with various brain areas, ZI may be able to carry out multiple physiological and behavioral functions synergistically.
source: Through convergent and divergent connectivity with various brain areas, ZI may be able to carry out multiple physiological and behavioral functions synergistically.

claim: Whisker deflection per se did not elicit significant locomotion of animals.
source: In our control experiments, the whisker deflection per se did not elicit significant locomotion of animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by control data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Loud noise sound (80 dB SPL) elicited animal running.
source: Loud noise sound (80 dB sound pressure level or SPL) elicited animal running, and the running speed was recorded in real time (Figure 1A, left).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The viral expression of opsins co-localized well with Cre-dependent tdTomato expression.
source: The viral expression of opsins co-localized well with Cre-dependent tdTomato expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating PV-specific expression of opsins.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Blue LED light evoked robust spiking in ChR2-expressing neurons.
source: The efficacies of ChR2 and ArchT were confirmed by slice whole-cell recordings showing that blue LED light evoked robust spiking in ChR2-expressing neurons and green LED light induced a strong hyperpolarization of the membrane potential in ArchT-expressing cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by slice recording data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Green LED light induced a strong hyperpolarization of the membrane potential in ArchT-expressing cells.
source: The efficacies of ChR2 and ArchT were confirmed by slice whole-cell recordings showing that blue LED light evoked robust spiking in ChR2-expressing neurons and green LED light induced a strong hyperpolarization of the membrane potential in ArchT-expressing cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by slice recording data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CNO increased the threshold for spiking and decreased the number of spikes evoked by current injections in hM4D(Gi)-expressing neurons.
source: The efficacy of DREADDi inhibition was confirmed by slice recording showing that CNO increased the threshold for spiking and decreased the number of spikes evoked by current injections (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by slice recording data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: PV+ neurons are GABAergic.
source: PV+ neurons in ZI are GABAergic (Barthó et al., 2002) and provide inhibition to their target neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.
